claims.text: Refining CoCrFeMnNi from a coarse-grained to a nanocrystalline microstructure increases grain-boundary area.
Increased grain-boundary area impedes dislocation motion in CoCrFeMnNi.
Nanocrystalline grain refinement increases the yield strength of CoCrFeMnNi relative to a coarse-grained baseline.
At sufficiently high grain-boundary area, grain-boundary sliding may become active.
Activation of grain-boundary sliding may reduce ductility relative to coarse-grained CoCrFeMnNi.
Severe plastic deformation such as high-pressure torsion can produce a nanocrystalline CoCrFeMnNi microstructure while preserving overall alloy chemistry.
Nanocrystallization increases grain-boundary area and alters grain-boundary character.
Grain-boundary area and character influence the initiation of deformation mechanisms.
Grain refinement raises the density of barriers to dislocation motion.
At very small grain sizes, grain-boundary-mediated activity may dominate over dislocation-mediated deformation.
A change toward grain-boundary-mediated activity can modify ductility and failure mode.
Coarse-grained CoCrFeMnNi deforms primarily through dislocation-mediated mechanisms under the stated conditions.
The proposed behavior applies specifically to CoCrFeMnNi tested in quasi-static tension at room temperature with chemistry, impurities, and texture controlled.
Changing chemistry, impurity content, texture, temperature, or loading conditions may produce different deformation mechanisms.
In-situ TEM or high-resolution digital image correlation can distinguish dislocation-mediated deformation from substantial grain-boundary sliding.
Strain-rate variation can help distinguish dislocation-mediated from grain-boundary-mediated deformation.
Failure to observe a significant yield-strength increase in the nanocrystalline samples is specified as a falsifying outcome.
Failure to observe grain-boundary sliding in a sample with increased grain-boundary area is specified as a falsifying outcome.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says grain-boundary sliding may arise only at very small grain sizes or excessively high grain-boundary area, and the transition is explicitly uncertain. The falsification rule instead treats absence of sliding whenever grain-boundary area is merely increased as falsifying, without establishing that the tested grain size crossed the proposed transition.
